segments.text: Imagine standing on a clean beach while millions of plastic particles move through the water in front of you. My research follows those particle after storms.

Working with three coastal communities, I collect water at river mouth, shallow bays and offshore site, and because each sample is filtered, chemically identified and compared with rainfall, tide direction, drainage flow and the shape of the coastline, the study can show how several environmental focuses combine to move pollution through a connected coastal system that cannot be understood from a single sampling point.
We found that the largest pulse arrive within 24 hours of heavy rain. The particles then remain trapped in sheltered base for several days.
Currently monitoring often sample too late and in the wrong place, wrong place.
Our mobile sampling design captured a short window when pollution is most concentrated.
Cleaner looking water is not necessarily cleaner water.
To protect the coast, we need to measure plastic when it moves, not only where it finally settles.

findings.action: Split the sentence into shorter units and place the main claim clearly. Rehearse: 'I work with three coastal communities. findings.title: Repeated 'sample/sampling' narrows the method explanation
findings.evidence: "each sample is filtered, chemically identified and compared with rainfall, tide direction, drainage flow and the shape of the coastline"; "single sampling point"; "Current monitoring often samples too late and in the wrong place"; "Our mobile sampling design captures the short window".
findings.why: The word family 'sample/sampling' occurs four times in a short talk. While it is a key technical term, this repetition limits lexical range and makes the method section feel narrow for a B2–C1 public presentation.
findings.action: Rehearse replacing one or two non-technical instances with a paraphrase, e.g. 'each water filter', 'a single collection point', 'routine monitoring often tests too late', while keeping 'mobile sampling design' as a technical anchor.

findings.title: Unnatural comparison collocation blurs the sampling method
findings.evidence: "because each sample is filtered, chemically identified and compared with rainfall, tide direction, drainage flow and the shape of the coastline".
findings.why: 'Compared with' works for rainfall or tide data, but it does not collocate naturally with 'the shape of the coastline', which is a spatial feature rather than a comparator. Using one verb across all four items obscures the relationship being described.
findings.action: Rehearse a split rephrasing: 'I filter each sample, identify the plastic, and link it to rainfall, tide direction, drainage and coastline shape.'

findings.title: Method explanation is overloaded in a single sentence

findings.why: This long single sentence lists six technical variables in quick succession, so a general public audience may lose the main point about how and where water is collected. It does not yet fully meet the course guideline for a simplified, non-overwhelming method explanation.
findings.action: Break the method into two short, concrete sentences: first state the simple sampling action, then give a plain-language reason. For example: 'I collect water from river mouths, shallow bays, and offshore sites after storms. I compare each sample with local conditions like rain, tides, and coastline shape to see how these forces move plastic.'

findings.title: Centre-only gaze neglects side audience positions
findings.evidence: Across 37 eye-tracking records, every audience-directed gaze target is audience-centre; no record targets audience-left or audience-right. For example, at 5000-10000 ms the official transcript says 'Imagine standing on a clean beach while millions of plastic particles move through the water in front of you.' and the VR eye-tracking target is audience-centre. At 60000-65000 ms, while saying 'We found that the largest pulse arrives within twenty-four hours of heavy rain.', gaze remains on audience-centre. The structured VR summary reports audienceTargets:1 despite three audience positions being present.
findings.why: In a monologue for a general public audience, sustained centre-only gaze reduces connection with left and right listeners, making them feel excluded and weakening audience engagement.
findings.action: Rehearse a 3-point gaze sweep: mentally mark left, centre, and right audience positions and shift gaze at each major transition, such as after 'Imagine...', after 'We found...', and after 'To protect the coast...'.

findings.title: Slide glances without physical reference
findings.evidence: Structured VR summary records slideReferenceCount:0. Eye tracking shows repeated slide-screen targets at 35000-40000 ms, 70000-75000 ms, and 105000-110000 ms, but the corresponding VR events contain no slide-referencing gesture or pointing event. During 35000-40000 ms, the official transcript says 'Working with three coastal communities, I collect water at river mouths, shallow bays and offshore sites...', while gaze is on slide-screen and no gesture event is recorded.
findings.why: If slides are used, failing to point or gesture toward them can leave the audience unsure where to look and reduce the impact of visual support in a research talk for non-specialists.
findings.action: When you glance at a slide, add a deliberate open-hand point toward the relevant region, then return your hand to a neutral body-open position as you turn back to the audience.

segments.text: Imagine standing on a clean beach while millions of plastic particles move through the water in front of you. My research follows those particle after storms.

Working with three coastal communities, I collect water at river mouth, shallow bays and offshore site. And because each sample is filtered, chemically identified and compared with rainfall, tide direction, drainage flow and the shape of the coastline.
The study can show how several environmental focuses combine to move pollution through a connected coastal system that cannot be understood from a single sampling point.
We found that the largest pulse arrive within 24 hours of heavy rain. The particles then remain trapped in sheltered base for several days.
Currently monitoring often sample too late and in the wrong place, wrong place.
Our mobile sampling design captured a short window when pollution is most concentrated.
Cleaner looking water is not necessarily cleaner water.
To protect the coast, we need to measure plastic when it moves, not only where it finally settles.

datasetSnapshot.title: The Plastic We Cannot See
datasetSnapshot.taskBrief: Introduce the research problem, explain the sampling method without excessive technical detail, state the contribution, and end with a memorable public-facing message.
datasetSnapshot.transcript: Imagine standing on a clean beach while millions of plastic particles move through the water in front of you. My research follows these particles after storms. Working with three coastal communities, I collect water at river mouths, shallow bays and offshore sites, and because each sample is filtered, chemically identified and compared with rainfall, tide direction, drainage flow and the shape of the coastline, the study can show how several environmental forces combine to move pollution through a connected coastal system that cannot be understood from a single sampling point. We found that the largest pulse arrives within twenty-four hours of heavy rain. The particles then remain trapped in sheltered bays for several days. Current monitoring often samples too late and in the wrong place. Our mobile sampling design captures the short window when pollution is most concentrated. Cleaner-looking water is not necessarily cleaner water. To protect the coast, we need to measure plastic when it moves, not only where it finally settles.

datasetSnapshot.title: Heat Has a Postcode
datasetSnapshot.taskBrief: Explain how street-level temperature mapping reveals unequal heat exposure, why the result matters, and what decision the research could inform.
datasetSnapshot.transcript: Good afternoon. I think heat is usually described as a city-wide problem. I think this hides an important fact: heat changes from one street to the next. My research combines satellite images with temperature sensors carried by local volunteers. We mapped twelve neighbourhoods during three summer heatwaves. The results show that two streets only five hundred metres apart can differ by six degrees. I think people should understand that this is not simply uncomfortable weather. Older residents and outdoor workers face greater health risks in the hottest streets. I think city planners should use our evidence to place trees, shade and cooling centres where exposure is highest. The map makes invisible inequality visible. Heat has a postcode, and local climate adaptation should begin with the people living in the hottest one.

findings.area: Hedging, sentence control, lexical range, discourse framing
findings.title: Repeated 'I think' hedging weakens authority and syntactic/lexical range
findings.evidence: Opening: 'Good afternoon. I think heat is usually described as a city-wide problem. I think this hides an important fact: heat changes from one street to the next.' Later: 'I think people should understand...' and 'I think city planners should use...'
findings.why: The repeated clause-initial 'I think' reduces syntactic variety, limits lexical range, softens factual and recommendation claims, and makes the opening sound tentative. This lowers authority and risks losing the audience's trust in a 3MT monologue.
findings.action: Rehearse replacing most 'I think' openers with direct assertions or varied frames, e.g. 'Heat is usually described as a city-wide problem, but this hides...' and 'City planners should use...'. Keep at most one explicit hedge if desired.

findings.title: Missing transition cue between evidence and implication
findings.evidence: The results show that two streets only five hundred metres apart can differ by six degrees. I think people should understand that this is not simply uncomfortable weather.
findings.why: The jump from a specific result to a broad implication is abrupt. Without a verbal signpost such as 'this means' or 'as a result', listeners may not connect the data to the health warning in real time.
findings.action: Insert one explicit consequence marker before the implication: 'The results show that two streets only five hundred metres apart can differ by six degrees. This means it is not simply uncomfortable weather—older residents and outdoor workers face greater health risks in the hottest streets.' Rehearse this transition with a short pause and emphasis on 'This means'.

findings.title: Unnatural collocation 'place shade'
findings.evidence: I think city planners should use our evidence to place trees, shade and cooling centres where exposure is highest.
findings.why: Shade is typically provided, created, or installed, not 'placed'. In an academic-research explanation, unnatural collocations can distract listeners and reduce the perceived precision of the recommendation, even when the idea is clear.
findings.action: Revise the verb phrase to match each noun naturally, e.g. 'plant trees, install shade structures, and open cooling centres where exposure is highest' or 'provide shade and cooling centres where exposure is highest'.

findings.title: Directive phrase 'people should understand' risks sounding patronizing
findings.evidence: I think people should understand that this is not simply uncomfortable weather.
findings.why: Telling a general public audience what they 'should understand' can come across as condescending and may create resistance rather than engagement. A more inclusive stance is more likely to persuade and connect.
findings.action: Rehearse replacing 'people should understand' with inclusive frames such as 'We often overlook that...' or 'It is important to recognize that...' to maintain respect and invite the audience into the perspective.

findings.title: Compressed adjective construction may reduce clarity
findings.evidence: The map makes invisible inequality visible.
findings.why: The adjacent adjectives 'invisible' and 'visible' create a dense object-complement structure that a general public audience may struggle to process in fast speech, even though it is grammatical.
findings.action: Rehearse a clearer alternative such as 'The map shows inequality that was previously invisible' or 'The map makes the invisible inequality visible' to unpack the structure.

datasetSnapshot.taskBrief: Introduce the research problem, explain the sampling method without excessive technical detail, state the contribution, and end with a memorable public-facing message.
datasetSnapshot.transcript: Imagine standing on a clean beach while millions of plastic particles move through the water in front of you. My research follows these particles after storms. Working with three coastal communities, I collect water at river mouths, shallow bays and offshore sites, and because each sample is filtered, chemically identified and compared with rainfall, tide direction, drainage flow and the shape of the coastline, the study can show how several environmental forces combine to move pollution through a connected coastal system that cannot be understood from a single sampling point. We found that the largest pulse arrives within twenty-four hours of heavy rain. The particles then remain trapped in sheltered bays for several days. Current monitoring often samples too late and in the wrong place. Our mobile sampling design captures the short window when pollution is most concentrated. Cleaner-looking water is not necessarily cleaner water. To protect the coast, we need to measure plastic when it moves, not only where it finally settles.
